yarn-dinkum.meaning: Every paragraph is carried across point for point: "I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge", "a seat at the mailing-desk, with eight quid every Saturday night", "there's no lift in the building", "a dollar's worth one hundred and six cents to a good businessman". The only drift is the currency: "eight quid" sits beside "sixty cents out of any dollar".
yarn-dinkum.sense: Terms fit: "native nous" for common sense, "making a mug of yourself" for making a fool, "the old man's loaded", "won't be a skerrick of real use", "if your expense accounts don't tell porkies", "the drapery business" for dry-goods. "mongrel steer" works for the scalawag steer.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural, unforced voice: "it fair makes a bloke hunch his shoulders", "Doesn't matter a scrap", "unless you're dead careful, son". "eight quid" is a slightly tourist move in an American letter, and "bloke" and "fella" alternate a lot.
yarn-dinkum.register: A moderate level-3 touch: "cos", "bloke", "uni", "loaded", "porkies", "skerrick" scattered through a text that otherwise keeps the old merchant's syntax; no swearing, within vulgarity 1. Perhaps a shade light for level 3.
yarn-dinkum.tone: The dry, paternal, mock-stern tone survives: "Course the bills won't break me, but they'll break you", "the Lord laid down for us", "Baron Munchausen was the first travelling salesman".
yarn-dinkum.flow: Reads smoothly: "There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building." Joins are clean throughout.
yarn-dinkum.variety: A good spread: "nous", "mug", "loaded", "skerrick", "porkies", "drapery", "Doesn't matter a scrap"; "bloke" recurs ("a bloke can start", "the bloke who hasn't licked stamps", "other bloke's talent") but is varied with "fella".
yarn-dinkum.essence: Unmistakably the Self-Made Merchant's letter: the steer simile, the stamp-licking, the talent in a napkin, the hundred-and-six-cent dollar all stand: "they'd swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin".

unharnessed.meaning: Mostly complete: "I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge outright", "eight dollars every Saturday night", "there's no lift in the building". The steer simile is garbled: "feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn" makes the weight belong to the fattening, not the feed.
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit their spots: "making a galah of yourself", "the old man's loaded and can wear it", "kept me mouth shut", "won't be a scrap of real use", "sweet-talk the other bloke's talent into it", "my reps' bills" for drummers.
unharnessed.authenticity: Sounds like a real Australian father: "it's enough to make a bloke go round-shouldered just looking at it", "can wear it, because he won't wear it once you're out of college", "It's all down to the man".
unharnessed.register: Level-3 weight: "galah", "loaded", "porkies", "me mouth", "lads" over the original structure, no swearing; within vulgarity 1. Perhaps a touch light.
unharnessed.tone: Keeps the wry paternal admonition: "Course, the bills won't send me broke, but they'll send you broke unless you're very, very careful."
unharnessed.flow: Smooth except the tangled steer line: "feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn".
unharnessed.variety: Varied: "galah", "wear it", "sure-fire", "the works", "sweet-talk", "reps"; "porkies" is used twice in one sentence: "aren't telling porkies; and they don't usually tell porkies".
unharnessed.essence: The letter's character and maxims survive whole: "a dollar's worth a hundred and six cents to a good businessman, and he never spends the dollar".

engine.meaning: Much of the original is left verbatim, but swaps break sense: "he is never able to realise more than sixty cents on any quid that comes to him. But a quid is worth one hundred and six cents to a good business man, and he never spends the dollar." Also "It is all with the bloke" and "the first travelling bloke" blur the original.
engine.sense: Several substitutions take the wrong sense or strain: "a quid is worth one hundred and six cents" (quid in a cents maxim), "the first travelling bloke" for traveling man (salesman), "the old bloke" for the old man (the firm's head), "It is all with the bloke".
engine.authenticity: Stock words bolted onto archaic prose: "very, dead careful", "a bloody good deal like feeding his weight in corn", "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things". The rest is unchanged nineteenth-century American ("run an automobile", "dry-goods business", "scalawag steer").
engine.register: Largely untranslated: "When I told you that I wished you to get a liberal education", "increased operating expenses", with a handful of swaps ("bloke", "uni", "lift", "quid"). "bloody" twice is within vulgarity 1 but the Aussie weight is well below level 3.
engine.tone: Mostly the original tone because mostly the original text, but "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things" breaks the measured paternal voice with an outburst the letter never has.
engine.flow: Clunky joins: "unless you are very, dead careful", "a bloody good deal like", "Bloody hell, I simply mention", "It is all with the bloke".
engine.variety: Leans on "bloke" over and over: "young blokes", "a bloke can get rich", "the old bloke", "the bloke who hasn't got it", "the bloke who hasn't licked stamps", "other bloke's talent", "It's the bloke who keeps saving", "travelling bloke".
engine.essence: Recognisable as the letter since most of it is verbatim ("there are others that you could start out with just a napkin"), but damaged spots like "a quid is worth one hundred and six cents" flatten its key maxim.

dinkum-3.meaning: Complete and accurate: "I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge", "feeding a no-hoper steer its own weight in corn when it won't fatten up", "eight quid every Saturday night", "Baron Munchausen was the first commercial traveller". "a broad education" for liberal is a fair gloss.
dinkum-3.sense: Mostly exact: "no-hoper steer", "kept my trap shut", "your own nous", "success on a plate", "heaps of room at the top". "a beaut education" strains, since the original's point is merely a good education, not a splendid one; "any quid ... one hundred and six cents" mixes currencies.
dinkum-3.authenticity: Sounds like a real Australian: "I tell ya, going over it fair makes a bloke's shoulders hunch up", "can wear it, cos he won't wear it once you've left uni", "commercial traveller" is the right local term for a travelling salesman.
dinkum-3.register: Squarely level 3: "mate", "cos", "trap shut", "loaded", "heaps", "skerrick", "sweet-talk" through a letter that keeps its shape; no swearing, within vulgarity 1.
dinkum-3.tone: The stern, dry, fatherly humour holds: "Now, the bills won't send me broke, of course, but they'll send you broke unless you're dead careful."
dinkum-3.flow: Smooth on the whole; one echo: "the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills still show his influence".
dinkum-3.variety: Broad and unrepeated: "no-hoper", "trap shut", "nous", "loaded", "wear it", "on a plate", "heaps", "beaut", "skerrick", "sweet-talk", "commercial traveller".
dinkum-3.essence: Unmistakably the letter: "Give some blokes a talent wrapped in a napkin to start out in business with, and they'll swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin".

yarn-troppo.meaning: Everything is here, with colour hung off the original: "Dead, dead careful.", "no matter what you shovel into him", "You'll have to take the stairs like everyone else.", "dynamite and all", "Every one of them reads like a fairy story." These elaborate rather than add facts.
yarn-troppo.sense: Terms fit: "rollin' in it and can wear it", "won't be worth a cracker to you", "Doesn't matter a skerrick", "aren't telling porkies", "get it into your noggin". "to live under the one roof" extends the original's "live together" aptly.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Mostly natural: "The cashier's just plonked your expense account for the month on my desk, son", "won't be worth a cracker". Some lines lean on stock tics: "I tell ya", "son", "my lad", "That's it. That's the lot."
yarn-troppo.register: A bit heavier than level 3, with extra address and asides: "son", "my lad", "mind", "mind you", "rollin' in it", "noggin"; no swearing, within vulgarity 1.
yarn-troppo.tone: The father's dry wit is kept but sometimes over-explained, which softens it: "Every one of them reads like a fairy story." spells out the Munchausen joke, and "You'll have to take the stairs like everyone else." glosses the lift line.
yarn-troppo.flow: Readable and punchy, though the added fragments chop the rhythm: "Dead, dead careful.", "That's it. That's the lot."
yarn-troppo.variety: Wide range: "plonked", "trap shut", "nous", "noggin", "rollin' in it", "skerrick", "worth a cracker", "porkies", "drapery", "into the bargain".
yarn-troppo.essence: Recognisably the letter, but the explanatory tags flatten its understatement: "There's plenty of room at the top here, mind, but there's no lift in the building. You'll have to take the stairs like everyone else."

yarn-dinkum.original: with eight dollars every Saturday night
yarn-dinkum.why: Converts the wage to quid while the later dollar-and-cents maxim stays in dollars, so the currency is inconsistent in an American letter.

yarn-dinkum.quote: a mongrel steer that won't fatten up
yarn-dinkum.original: a scalawag steer that won't fat up
yarn-dinkum.why: Fine choice, though "mongrel" leans to bad-tempered more than worthless; a small shift.

unharnessed.quote: feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn
unharnessed.original: a good deal like feeding his weight in corn to a scalawag steer that won't fat up
unharnessed.why: The reordering garbles the simile: it now reads as the steer failing to fatten up its own weight, losing the point that the steer eats its weight in feed.

unharnessed.quote: aren't telling porkies; and they don't usually tell porkies
unharnessed.original: if your expense accounts don't lie; and they generally don't lie in that particular way
unharnessed.why: Repeats "porkies" within the sentence where the original's repetition of "lie" could have been varied; slight echo.

engine.quote: unless you are very, dead careful
engine.original: unless you are very, very careful
engine.why: Mechanical swap of one "very" leaves a broken phrase no one would say.

engine.quote: Bloody hell, I simply mention these things
engine.why: An outburst bolted onto a calm sentence; nothing in the original prompts it and it jars the tone.

engine.quote: But a quid is worth one hundred and six cents to a good business man, and he never spends the dollar.
engine.original: But a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents to a good business man, and he never spends the dollar.
engine.why: Quid in a cents maxim is nonsense, and the sentence then reverts to "dollar", breaking the point.

engine.original: Baron Munchausen was the first traveling man
engine.why: "traveling man" means travelling salesman; "travelling bloke" loses the joke about salesmen's padded bills.

engine.quote: It's the bloke who keeps saving up and expenses down
engine.original: It's the man who keeps saving up and expenses down
engine.why: Representative of the relentless "bloke" substitution throughout.

engine.quote: a bloody good deal like feeding his weight in corn
engine.original: a good deal like feeding his weight in corn
engine.why: Intensifier dropped into an idiom where it adds nothing and sounds forced.

dinkum-3.why: "beaut" means splendid; the original is merely good, so the term overstates and sounds a little forced.

dinkum-3.quote: he never gets more than sixty cents out of any quid that comes his way
dinkum-3.original: he is never able to realize more than sixty cents on any dollar
dinkum-3.why: Quid paired with cents mixes currencies.

dinkum-3.quote: the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills
dinkum-3.original: the first traveling man, and my drummers' bills
dinkum-3.why: Repeats the phrase where the original varies "traveling man" and "drummers".

yarn-troppo.quote: You'll have to take the stairs like everyone else.
yarn-troppo.original: There is plenty of room at the top here, but there is no elevator in the building.
yarn-troppo.why: Explains the joke the original leaves dry, blunting it.

yarn-troppo.quote: Every one of them reads like a fairy story.
yarn-troppo.original: my drummers' bills still show his influence.
yarn-troppo.why: Spells out the Munchausen punchline, flattening the understatement.

yarn-troppo.original: with eight dollars every Saturday night
yarn-troppo.why: Wage in quid while the later maxim stays in dollars and cents; inconsistent currency.
Added tag that renders nothing and pads the paragraph.

summaries.yarn-dinkum: A faithful, smooth, lightly Aussie retelling that keeps the letter whole; slightly light for level 3, with a small currency wobble.
summaries.unharnessed: Natural and idiomatic with good Aussie choices; one garbled simile and a repeated term keep it a notch below the best.
summaries.engine: Mostly the untranslated original with mechanical swaps that break phrases and the money maxim; the weakest candidate.
summaries.dinkum-3: The most rounded candidate: idiomatic, on the brief, faithful and varied, with only small strains.
summaries.yarn-troppo: Lively and varied with good idiom, but a shade heavy and prone to explaining the original's dry jokes.
